‘High on Coke’: Elon Musk stunned by Berkshire’s dividend payout. Learn how to build your own passive income stream now

Tesla CEO Elon Musk is no stranger to eye-popping sums of money. After all, he currently holds the title of the world's wealthiest person, with his wealth fluctuating around $1 trillion since SpaceX's June IPO (1).

But even for Musk, some financial figures are enough to raise an eyebrow.

A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change

For instance, Berkshire Hathaway's 2022 annual report revealed that the investment empire earned $704 million in dividends that year from its Coca-Cola holdings (2). Upon hearing the news, Musk couldn't resist commenting on X, "Berkshire Hathaway [is] high on Coke (3)."

That figure was calculated based on Berkshire's roughly 400 million shares in Coca-Cola and the 44 cents per share that Coca-Cola paid out in quarterly dividends in 2022 (4).

Fast-forward to 2026, and that dividend payout has climbed even higher. According to Berkshire's latest 13F filing for the second quarter of 2026, the company still holds 400 million shares in Coca-Cola (5). With Coca-Cola having raised its 2026 dividend to $2.12 per share (6), Berkshire is estimated to collect an impressive $848 million in dividend income for the year.

As the former CEO of Berkshire Hathaway, Warren Buffett has long expressed his love for Coca-Cola.

On a 2019 Squawk Box episode, Buffett shared with CNBC, "I drink probably five 12-ounce Cokes a day, and that's about 700 calories, and I've been doing it more or less my whole life. I can't imagine anybody that feels better than I do (7)."

Beyond his appreciation for the taste, Buffett's Coca-Cola investment became a remarkable source of passive income for the company — and you can learn from his strategy when building your own portfolio.

Here are three takeaways to consider on your path to passive income.

Dividend stocks

Investing in the stock market has never been more accessible, allowing everyday investors to earn passive income through dividend-paying stocks — just like Buffett. Companies that consistently pay dividends enable investors to earn income without having to sell their shares.

See? If you invested in the company 15 years ago, you would have increased the value of your stake some 282-fold. The company itself was recently valued at $1.4 trillion.

The story is a little different over the past five years, though, which feature slower growth and some loss of value. But what matters most to most investors should be what's ahead, not behind -- so how should you expect Tesla to grow over the coming decade?

No one can know exactly how Tesla will do. But let's make an educated and somewhat conservative guess. Over many decades, the stock market has averaged annual gains of close to 10%. Tesla could be expected to generally outperform that. If you plunk $1,000 into Tesla now and the stock grows at, say, 18% annually, your stake will be worth $5,234 a decade hence.

How accurate is that estimate?

Not very. Tesla might grow more slowly because:

Its operating profit margin has been shrinking recently.

Its valuation is arguably quite steep -- with a recent forward-looking price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 152, well above the five-year average of 78.

It's facing competition, from Chinese EV maker BYD and others.

But it might also grow briskly because:

Its Cybercab business could take off, as might its Optimus humanoid robots.

Tesla has a formidable cash cushion, which can help it build new businesses, such as its robotaxis.

It might get favorable regulatory treatment. In Texas, for instance, it got a 50% tax break on its $10 billion solar factory.

Since Tesla is involved in so many dynamic businesses, it's very hard to estimate where it will be in a decade. A 4.2x return looks like a sensible estimate, at least.

title: Nine Years, Eight Delays, and Now Rocket Thrusters: Tesla Finally Sets a Roadster Date
detail:
Nine Years, Eight Delays, and Now Rocket Thrusters: Tesla Finally Sets a Roadster Date
Sheryar Siddiq
Sat, September 19, 2026 at 9:11 PM CDT 5 min read
TSLA
Trade Tesla on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Tesla, Inc. (NASDAQ:TSLA) has once again set a deadline for its second-generation Roadster. This time, the automaker says October 1 is real, and it's accompanied by rocket-launch visuals and a technology package sourced directly from Elon Musk's other company, SpaceX.

A Nine-Year Wait

The Roadster was first exhibited as a prototype in November 2017, with startling numbers claimed at the time: a 1.9-second 0-60 mph time, a top speed of 250+ mph, and a range of around 620 miles from a 200-kWh battery. Production was originally scheduled for 2020, with deposits ranging from $50,000 to the full $250,000 for the "Founders Series" model. That timeframe has subsequently moved repeatedly, from 2020 to 2022 to 2023 and beyond, including a widely mocked April 1 demo date Musk set at last November's shareholder meeting, which he later revealed he chose primarily to provide "deniability" if it slipped again. It did, moving to late April, then "a month or so," and finally in August. October 1 is the latest in at least five Roadster demo or unveiling timelines floated this year.

A More Specific Announcement This Time

This time, the announcement includes more specifics. Tesla, Inc. (NASDAQ:TSLA) put "Go for Launch" on X around September 12, along with a teaser image of the car's rear three-quarter view marked with the date "10.01." A countdown clock appeared on Tesla's Roadster order page at the same time, as did formal invites to a gathering in Waco, Texas, which are non-transferable and exclusive to reservation holders.

According to reports, the car has evolved significantly behind the scenes: Tesla, Inc. (NASDAQ:TSLA) reportedly abandoned earlier plans to base the production Roadster on Model S Plaid components in favor of an all-new carbon-fiber hypercar platform, resulting in a more exotic and fundamentally different vehicle than what reservation holders initially put down deposits for in 2017.

The SpaceX Package

The main focus of the unveiling is expected to be what Musk has referred to as the "SpaceX package" since 2018: a set of cold-gas thrusters, small nozzles that fire compressed gas rather than burning rocket fuel, built around hardware borrowed from SpaceX's Falcon 9 program, internally code-named A71, and using the same composite overwrapped pressure vessel tank design. Musk claims a thruster-equipped Roadster could reach 60 mph in around 1.1 seconds and that the mechanism could hypothetically lift the vehicle off the ground. Tesla originally claimed a 1.9-second 0-60 time for the 2017 Roadster prototype, although the heavily redesigned production version may carry different specifications. Notably, reports indicate that the thruster-equipped variation may not be street legal and may be sold as a limited run on the track, implying that Tesla's headline performance claim could refer to a product that most consumers will never be able to drive on public roads.

It has been a roller-coaster ride for Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA) stock in recent years. In 2021, the stock reached a high of roughly $400 per share, only to collapse to nearly $100 per share in 2023. The stock then surged above $400 in 2025, only to collapse once again below $250 that same year.

After yet another surge and correction, Tesla stock currently hovers around $350 per share, resulting in a $1.1 trillion market cap. Through it all, Cathie Wood's firm, Ark Invest, never sold out of its Tesla stake. The position has been trimmed and added to many times over the years. But the firm has always remained a strong Tesla bull.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

With a position valued at $1 billion, Tesla remains one of Ark Invest's largest holdings across all its funds. It's no wonder. Ark Invest currently has a long-term price target of $4,600 per share for Tesla stock. That's a sizable increase from its earlier price target of just $3,000 per share. In either case, Ark Invest is adamant that Tesla can deliver 1,000% gains for patient shareholders.

Ark Invest's Cathie Wood. Image source: Getty Images.

Why does Cathie Wood still believe in Tesla? It all likely comes down to one key catalyst.

This is why Cathie Wood still loves Tesla stock

Wood's firm no longer views Tesla as a simple EV (electric vehicle) stock. Instead, she believes the company will soon be a robotaxi juggernaut. With unmatched vertical integration, Tesla is positioned to scale its robotaxi fleet rapidly, at a lower cost than most competitors. The company's aggressive investments in artificial intelligence and self-driving technology, meanwhile, grant it the opportunity to convert its existing manufacturing capacity to robotaxi production while minimizing reliance on outside vendors.

"One of the biggest potential markets that we see in AI is autonomous driving and we think that all vehicles in the future, all passenger cars will be electric," a report from Ark Invest concludes. "We think $8 trillion to $10 trillion for the entire autonomous taxi opportunity throughout the world, from almost nothing," is possible, Wood adds. "That's how quickly AI is going to cause these things to happen."

The robotaxi opportunity alone accounts for 90% of Ark Invest's long-term price prediction for Tesla. In short, the firm is all-in on Tesla's robotaxi ambitions.

title: Delivery Outlook Shows Tesla (TSLA)’s Core Business Under Pressure. Its Next Growth Engine Must Deliver
detail:
Delivery Outlook Shows Tesla (TSLA)’s Core Business Under Pressure. Its Next Growth Engine Must Deliver
Abdul Rahman
Sat, September 19, 2026 at 12:14 PM CDT 3 min read
TSLA
Trade Tesla on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Goldman Sachs has cut its delivery forecast for Tesla, Inc. (NASDAQ:TSLA) while citing weaker sales trends across the company's most important markets. The investment bank slashed its Q3 delivery forecast to 435,000 vehicles from 490,000. It also lowered its Q4 delivery forecast to 475,000 vehicles from 515,000.

The question now is whether Tesla's demand weakness is temporary or signals a deeper problem. Either way, investors want to see greater contribution from Tesla's other growth initiatives.

Goldman's Delivery Cut Exposes Demand Problem in Key Markets

Goldman's delivery forecast revision points to weakness across key markets. The bank has noted that monthly and weekly sales in China, the US, and Europe are tracking below earlier expectations.

Delivery Outlook Shows Tesla (TSLA)’s Core Business Under Pressure. Its Next Growth Engine Must Deliver

Goldman's new Q3 delivery projection is below the consensus estimate of 456,000 vehicles, while the new Q4 forecast is still above the consensus estimate of 462,000.

That makes the Q4 an important test of whether the weakness is temporary.

If production and demand improve as the Model Y L becomes more widely available, that could validate a temporary-weakness argument. However, if deliveries remain weak despite the product ramp and seasonal support, Tesla would face a more difficult explanation over its growth trajectory.

Tesla's Next Growth Engine Must Deliver More Than Promises

As the core vehicle business shows weakness, Tesla, Inc. (NASDAQ:TSLA)'s investment case increasingly depends on its autonomy initiatives stimulating growth. The Full Self-Driving (FSD) system and the Cybercab robotaxi are central to that transition.

Cybercab has moved from a concept toward commercial deployment, with Tesla offering robotaxi services in Austin, Texas. However, the Cybercab rollout has been met by regulatory scrutiny as the program uses cars without a steering wheel or pedals. NHTSA is investigating whether Tesla properly self-certified the vehicle as compliant with applicable federal motor vehicle safety standards.

NHTSA scrutiny of the Cybercab rollout underscores the challenge Tesla faces in scaling its robotaxi business to unlock another growth engine.

Tesla needs newer products and autonomy-related services to drive the next phase of its growth. If core vehicle business continues to weaken while FSD and Cybercab adoption develops slowly, Tesla's transition to new growth drivers could take longer and cost more than investors expect.

Investor Positioning Reflects a Divided Outlook

According to Insider Monkey's database, institutional positioning in Tesla, Inc. (NASDAQ:TSLA) provides a mixed signal. The number of hedge funds holding Tesla shares decreased to 116 in Q2 from 123 in Q1. Among major holders, BAMCO increased its stake 5% to 12.5 million shares, D. E. Shaw reduced its position to 4.3 million shares, while Holocene Advisors held its position at 3.6 million shares.
